title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: When they got up from the table, Levin walked with Gagin through the high-ceilinged room toward the billiard room, feeling his arms swing with a peculiar lightness as he went. Crossing the big room, he ran into his father-in-law.
"Well, how do you like our Temple of Indolence?" the prince said, taking his arm. "Come on, come on!"
"Yes, I wanted to walk around and look at everything. It's interesting."

"Yes, it's interesting for you. But for me the interest is quite different. Take a look at those little old men there," he said, pointing to a club member with a hunched back and jutting lower lip, shuffling toward them in soft boots, "and try to imagine they were _shlupiks_ like that from birth."
"What do you mean, _shlupiks_?"

"I see you don't know the term. It's our club word. You know the egg-rolling game—when an egg has been rolled long enough, it becomes a _shlupik_. Same with us: a man keeps coming and coming to the club, and ends up a _shlupik_. Ah, you laugh! But we watch ourselves to be sure we don't slide into it. Do you know Prince Tchetchensky?" the prince asked; and Levin could see from his face that he was about to tell something funny.
"No, I don't."

"You don't say! Well, Prince Tchetchensky is quite a name around here. Never mind, though. He's always playing billiards. Just three years ago he wasn't a _shlupik_, still kept his spirits up, and even used to call other people _shlupiks_. But one day he comes in, and our porter—you know Vassily? The fat one, famous for his _bon mots_—well, Prince Tchetchensky asks him, 'Come, Vassily, who's here? Any _shlupiks_ yet?' And he says, 'You're the third.' Yes, my dear boy, he really did say it!"

Talking and greeting people they ran into, Levin and the prince walked through all the rooms: the great hall where the tables were already set up and the regulars were playing for small stakes; the divan room, where men were playing chess, and Sergey Ivanovitch sat talking to someone; the billiard room, where a lively group around a sofa in a recess was drinking champagne—Gagin among them. They glanced into the "infernal regions," where a crowd of men was gathered around one table with Yashvin in the middle. Trying not to make any noise, they walked into the dim reading room, where under shaded lamps a young man with an angry expression was flipping through one journal after another, and a bald general sat absorbed in a book. They also looked into what the prince called the intellectual room, where three gentlemen were caught up in a heated debate about the latest political news.

"Prince, please come, we're ready," said one of his card partners, who had come looking for him, and the prince went off. Levin sat down and listened, but recalling all the morning's talk, he was suddenly and terribly bored. He got up quickly and went to find Oblonsky and Turovtsin, whose company had been so pleasant.
Turovtsin was part of the group drinking in the billiard room, and Stepan Arkadyevitch was talking with Vronsky by the door at the far corner of the room.
"It's not that she's bored; it's this undefined, unsettled position," Levin caught, and was on the point of slipping away, but Stepan Arkadyevitch called out to him.

"Levin," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, and Levin noticed his eyes were not full of tears exactly, but moist—as they always got whenever he was drinking, or whenever he was moved. Just now, both. "Levin, don't go," he said, and squeezed his arm warmly above the elbow, clearly determined not to let him leave.

"This is a true friend of mine—almost my closest," he said to Vronsky. "You've become even closer and dearer to me. And I want you—and I think you ought—to be friends too, real friends, because you're both splendid fellows."
"Well, all that's left is for us to kiss and make up," Vronsky said with good-humored playfulness, holding out his hand.
Levin quickly took the offered hand and pressed it warmly.
"I'm very, very glad," said Levin.
"Waiter, a bottle of champagne," said Stepan Arkadyevitch.
"And I'm very glad," said Vronsky.
But despite Stepan Arkadyevitch's wish, and their own, they had nothing to talk about, and both of them felt it.
"Do you know, he's never met Anna?" Stepan Arkadyevitch said to Vronsky. "And there's nothing I want more than to take him to see her. Come on, Levin!"
"Really?" said Vronsky. "She'll be very glad to see you. I'd be heading home right now," he added, "but I'm worried about Yashvin, and I want to stay until he finishes."
"Why—is he losing?"
"He keeps losing, and I'm the only friend who can hold him back."
"Well, how about a game of pyramids? Levin, will you play? Excellent!" said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "Get the table ready," he told the marker.
"It's been ready a long while," answered the marker, who had already racked the balls in a triangle and was knocking the red one about to amuse himself.
"Right, let's start."
After the game Vronsky and Levin sat down at Gagin's table, and at Stepan Arkadyevitch's suggestion Levin joined the game.

Vronsky sat down at the table, with friends constantly coming up to him. Every now and then he stepped over to the "infernal" to keep an eye on Yashvin. Levin was enjoying a wonderful sense of rest after the mental fatigue of the morning. He was glad the hostility with Vronsky was over, and the feeling of calm, decorum, and comfort stayed with him.
When the game ended, Stepan Arkadyevitch took Levin's arm.
"Well, let's go to Anna's, then. Right now? Eh? She's at home. I promised her ages ago I'd bring you. Where were you planning to spend the evening?"
"Oh, nowhere in particular. I promised Sviazhsky I'd go to the Society of Agriculture. By all means, let's go," said Levin.
"Very good; come on. Find out if my carriage is here," Stepan Arkadyevitch told the waiter.

Levin went over to the table, paid the forty roubles he had lost, paid his bill—the total of which had somehow been mysteriously tallied by the little old waiter standing at the counter—and swinging his arms, walked back through all the rooms to the exit.
